title: Plain-English explainer of credential vaulting for agents: a partitioned vault plus a guard agent hands out placeholder tokens that are swapped for the real password/card at the last second, so the chat agent never sees secrets

claims: The agent you talk to never sees or touches the password or credit card number
Secrets live in a separate, encrypted, partitioned vault (possibly a separate VM)
A second 'security agent' guards the vault and approves or denies token requests
The agent is given a placeholder token ('IOU') and the security layer swaps in the real secret just before the request leaves the machine
This is how it works on Muse, Instinct and 'anywhere'; claims that agents read your passwords are misinformation
on_screen_only: Title card: 'AI Explained: How Agents Use Your Password Without Seeing It'
Talking head only; no UI, URLs or repos
cta: Let me know if you have more questions

relevance.why: Good architecture vocabulary (vault + policy agent + placeholder token substitution) if Haji ever builds an agent that handles user payment/credentials; otherwise explainer content.

implement_score.why: Pattern is worth copying if building an agent that pays or logs in on a user's behalf: keep secrets in a separate service, give the LLM only opaque placeholders, substitute at the egress proxy. Doable with an existing secrets manager; not needed for current apps.

verify: The 'it works this way everywhere' claim is overstated: many hobby agent setups put API keys straight in the LLM's environment
Which products actually implement a guard agent + egress substitution vs. a plain secrets store?

gap.what: Adds the egress-time secret substitution / placeholder-token design pattern for agents that handle credentials; liked set only covered app auth hygiene and prompt-injection warnings.
